A sense resistor produces a tiny voltage, often only tens of millivolts.
If the amplifier that reads it is far away, that faint signal must cross a noisy board and picks up more noise the farther it goes.
The best fix is to amplify the signal right at the resistor, so the long trip carries a strong signal.
Think of a whisper across a loud party. The farther the listener stands, the more the party noise drowns the whisper.
Handing the speaker a megaphone right where they stand fixes it, because the party noise stays the same but the voice is far louder.
The injected 2. 4 millivolts (0. 24 milliamps across 10 ohms) is 6 % of the raw signal but only 0. 12 % after a gain of 50.
Every doubling of gain before the long run halves the error. Noise coupled after the gain stage is not magnified.
Sense signal: the small voltage across the sense resistor, proportional to current. Current sense amplifier: a chip that multiplies that small voltage to a larger one.
Gain: how many times an amplifier multiplies a signal. Noise pickup: unwanted voltage a long wire collects from nearby switching. It depends on the wire, not on the signal.
Ground offset: two "ground" points on a board differ slightly in voltage when current flows through the copper between them.
A 5 milliohms resistor carries 8 amps, so the signal is 8 times 0. 005 = 40 millivolts. Say the long wire picks up 2. 4 millivolts of noise. That is 2. 4 / 40 = 6% of the signal.
Now put an amplifier with a gain of 50 at the resistor. The signal sent down the wire is 50 times 40 millivolts = 2 volts. The wire still picks up the same 2.
4 millivolts, which is now only 0. 12% of the signal. The signal-to-noise ratio (signal size divided by noise size) improved 50 times.
That is the whole idea: make the signal big before it travels.
"The long run is the weak point, because a millivolt-level signal picks up noise in proportion to length and the noise doesn't care how big the signal is.
So I'd move the amplifier to the resistor: a gain of 50 improves signal-to-noise on the long run by 34 decibels, and I send a volt-level, low-impedance signal, or digital data from a power monitor.
If I can't, I'd route the raw pair tight, matched and over a plane, filter at the far end, and make sure the amplifier's ground reference ties to the resistor's low side."
